PS1 — Currencies: intraday descriptive statistics¶

The three EBS pairs required by the homework, over one full session (2012-01-25, 09:30–16:00):

pair ~rate quoted in
major EUR/USD 1.297 → 1.311 USD per EUR
major USD/JPY 78.06 → 77.74 JPY per USD
cross EUR/JPY 101.26 → 101.94 JPY per EUR

They are not three independent instruments: EUR/JPY is the product of the other two, which is what makes part (l) possible.

fx.py replays the EBS level-update feed into a limit order book and hands back the same objects mbo.py produces for the equities, so hfstats.py computes parts (a)–(k) for both panels from a single definition.

Four features of this feed shape everything below, and differ sharply from ITCH:

  1. Level updates, not orders. A message says "this side, this price, now holds this much"; SIZE = 0 removes the level. There are no order ids, so there is no add/cancel count to report — which is why the homework asks for order counts on ITCH only. What we can count is messages, and those net together an unknown number of dealer actions.
  2. The book is capped at ten levels a side. Depth past the tenth level is not missing from the file, it is unobservable. Every depth number here is a lower bound in a way the ITCH numbers are not.
  3. Timestamps are stamped to 100 ms, against nanoseconds for ITCH, and many updates share one. The book is snapshotted once per timestamp, after the whole batch carrying it has been applied — applying updates one at a time invents crossed books the feed never showed.
  4. The trade tape lags the book. Matched at a print's own timestamp, only 47% of EUR/USD prints sit at or outside the touch and buys average just 0.33 spreads above sells — implausible for a market with no hidden liquidity. Backing the match up 200 ms gives 85% and 0.91 spreads, and 200 ms is the optimum on all three pairs independently. fx.LAG applies that offset.
In [1]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import fx
import hfstats as hs
import plots
from hfstats import FREQS, MINUTE, summary

books = fx.load()
eurusd, usdjpy, eurjpy = (books[p] for p in fx.PAIRS)

books
Out[1]:
{'EUR/USD': <Book EUR/USD: 14,535 trades, 58,316 quote updates>,
 'USD/JPY': <Book USD/JPY: 6,041 trades, 31,436 quote updates>,
 'EUR/JPY': <Book EUR/JPY: 1,542 trades, 34,360 quote updates>}

The three pairs¶

Sizes are in millions of the base currency (EUR for EUR/USD and EUR/JPY, USD for USD/JPY) — EBS quotes in millions and every size in the file is a whole number of them. dollar volume converts to USD millions, which for EUR/JPY needs the EUR/USD mid prevailing at each print.

The ordering is the one FX microstructure predicts: the two majors are cheaper and far more active than the cross, and EUR/JPY — which can always be manufactured from the other two — is the widest of the three.

In [2]:
overview = pd.DataFrame({
    p: {
        "tick size": b.tick,
        "trades": len(b.trades),
        "volume (mm base)": b.trades["size"].sum(),
        "dollar volume (USD mm)": b.trades.value.sum(),
        "quote updates": len(b.quotes),
        "mean spread (ticks)": b.grid.spread.mean() / b.tick,
        "mean spread (bps)": (1e4 * b.grid.spread / b.grid.mid).mean(),
        "mean BBO depth (mm)": (b.grid.bid_sz + b.grid.ask_sz).mean(),
        "mean book depth (mm)": (b.grid.bid_tot + b.grid.ask_tot).mean(),
        "crossed batches": b.n_crossed,
    } for p, b in books.items()
})
overview.round(3)

Data quality¶

Two things worth stating before the statistics rest on them.

Momentary crossed books. Applying a timestamp's updates as one batch removes almost all crossing, but 153 EUR/USD batches (0.2%), 65 USD/JPY and 3 EUR/JPY still leave the book locked or crossed. These are blanked out of the quote and grid frames rather than repaired, so they show up as the small NaN share below.

Trade signs. The aggressor flag is the exchange's own label and is used as the sign. sign_disagrees counts prints whose price sits on the far side of the 200 ms-prior mid from that flag — the residual disagreement after correcting for the tape lag, and a fair measure of how much of the signing is genuinely uncertain.

In [3]:
pd.DataFrame({
    p: {
        "grid seconds": len(b.grid),
        "grid NaN (%)": 100 * b.grid.mid.isna().mean(),
        "trades with no prior quote": int(b.trades.mid.isna().sum()),
        "sign disagrees with quote (%)": 100 * b.trades.sign_disagrees.mean(),
        "buys at/above prior ask (%)": 100 * b.trades.eval("sign == 1 and price >= ask").sum()
                                       / max((b.trades["sign"] == 1).sum(), 1),
        "sells at/below prior bid (%)": 100 * b.trades.eval("sign == -1 and price <= bid").sum()
                                        / max((b.trades["sign"] == -1).sum(), 1),
    } for p, b in books.items()
}).round(2)

Part (b) — number of trades and messages per minute¶

Trades are prints on the deal feed. updates and deletes are book messages — not order counts, for the reason given at the top; the homework restricts order counts to ITCH precisely because EBS cannot supply them. The delete share is still informative as the EBS analogue of a cancel-to-add ratio.

Part (f) — depth within twice the day's average spread¶

Size resting within one average spread either side of the mid, i.e. inside a band of twice the day's mean quoted spread. The best bid sits half the prevailing spread from the mid, so the band is empty exactly when the spread exceeds twice its average — frac_empty reports how often that happens.

Part (g) — 5-second price impact per minute¶

Within each minute, regress the 5-second midquote return following each print on the sign of that print:

$$10^4 \cdot \log\!\big(m_{t+5s}/m_t\big) \;=\; \alpha + \lambda \, s_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad s_t \in \{-1, +1\}$$

$\lambda$ is the midquote move a buy pushes through, in basis points. Minutes with fewer than ten prints, or with trades on only one side, cannot identify it and are dropped — which for EUR/JPY removes almost the whole session, so its impact estimate rests on very few minutes and should be read with that in mind.

The mean of per-minute slopes weights a thin minute as much as a busy one. The pooled alternative — every print in the session in one regression, with Newey–West standard errors for the overlapping 5-second windows — is the single number an economist would quote, and it comes with a t-statistic.

Part (j) — realized variance¶

$RV = \sum_t r_t^2$ over the session. Two separate microstructure effects show up here and they push in opposite directions, so it is worth separating them.

  • Across series, at a fixed frequency: transaction RV exceeds midquote RV (EUR/USD at 1s: 2927 vs 2320 bps²). That is bid–ask bounce — consecutive prints straddle the spread, adding variance the mid never sees.
  • Across frequencies, for the midquote: RV rises as sampling coarsens rather than falling. That is the reverse of the usual equity signature, and the cause is in the next cell: at one second the mid simply has not moved yet.

Volatility signature¶

RV of the midquote against the interval it is sampled at. For a price contaminated by bid–ask bounce this curve falls as the interval lengthens; here it rises for both majors, roughly doubling for USD/JPY between one second and five minutes.

The reason is in the last column: at one-second sampling 43% of EUR/USD seconds and 64% of USD/JPY seconds carry a midquote return of exactly zero. With a spread of about one pip and a tick a tenth that size, the EBS mid is a coarse, sticky object — over one second it usually has not moved at all. Those zeros drag the high-frequency RV below the true variance, and the shortfall unwinds as sampling coarsens and each interval contains at least one real quote revision.

So at one second these pairs are dominated by price discreteness and stale quotes, not by the bounce that dominates a comparable equity series. The bounce is still present — it is what separates the transaction column from the midquote column at any given frequency — but it is the smaller of the two effects on the mid.

In [17]:
_freqs = ["1s", "2s", "5s", "10s", "30s", MINUTE, "2min", "5min"]


def _signature(series):
    """RV in bps^2, and the share of intervals with no price change, by frequency."""
    out = {}
    for fq in _freqs:
        r = np.log(series.resample(fq).last().ffill().dropna()).diff().dropna()
        out[fq] = {"RV (bps^2)": 1e8 * (r ** 2).sum(), "zero returns (%)": 100 * (r == 0).mean()}
    return pd.DataFrame(out).T


pd.concat({p: _signature(b.grid.mid) for p, b in books.items()},
          axis=1, names=["pair", ""]).round(1)

Part (k) — autocorrelation of returns¶

Box–Pierce $Q$ tests whether the first $k$ autocorrelations are jointly zero; the ACF and PACF show where any dependence sits. The thing to look for is bid–ask bounce: a negative lag-1 autocorrelation in transaction returns that is absent, or much weaker, in midquote returns, and that fades as the sampling interval lengthens past the point where consecutive observations straddle the spread.

Part (l) — triangular arbitrage¶

EUR/JPY can be traded directly or manufactured through the dollar, so the two prices must agree. Buying a synthetic euro means paying the EUR/USD ask and then the USD/JPY ask; selling one means taking both bids:

$$\text{synthetic ask} = a_{\text{EUR/USD}} \cdot a_{\text{USD/JPY}}, \qquad \text{synthetic bid} = b_{\text{EUR/USD}} \cdot b_{\text{USD/JPY}}$$

which leaves two ways to be paid, each needing all three legs at once:

  • direct cheap — buy EUR/JPY at its ask, sell the synthetic: $\text{synth bid} - a_{\text{EUR/JPY}}$
  • direct rich — sell EUR/JPY at its bid, buy the synthetic: $b_{\text{EUR/JPY}} - \text{synth ask}$

Quantity is set by the thinnest leg, with every leg converted to millions of euro — so it is the size of the round trip that can be put on, not the size of any one quote. All three feeds are sampled on the common one-second clock the homework asks for.

In [19]:
tri = fx.triangular(books)
fx.triangular_summary(tri).round(4)

Are these real, or artefacts?¶

Two ways the headline number could be spurious, both checked rather than assumed.

Stale quotes. Sampling three independently-updating feeds on a common clock can line up quotes that were never simultaneously live. If that drove the result, the opportunity seconds would sit behind older quotes than average. They sit behind newer ones — the median stalest leg is 1.4 s at an opportunity against 2.1 s across all seconds — so the deviations arrive when the market is moving, not when it is asleep. That is the opposite of the staleness signature.

Costs and latency. Charging each round trip a few EUR/JPY ticks stands in crudely for brokerage and for the slippage of legging three books. The count decays smoothly rather than collapsing, which is what a real but thin edge looks like.

Intraday plots¶

The liquidity measures — spread, BBO depth and price impact — per five-minute interval, then the variance and lag-1 autocorrelation of one-minute transaction returns per thirty-minute interval, then the ACF of each return series to ten lags. Summary statistics table¶

The homework asks for one table: every part at the daily level, one column per pair. Parts (a)–(g) are the mean of their per-minute values, so each row is the average minute; (h)–(k) are whole-session figures at both sampling frequencies. hfstats.headline builds the same column for the equities, so the two panels stack into one table. Levels are comparable within this panel; against the equities only the relative rows — spreads in basis points, realized variance, autocorrelations — mean the same thing, because sizes here are millions of base currency, not shares.

Observations¶

1. The liquidity ordering is exactly the one the triangle implies. EUR/USD quotes at 0.86 bps, USD/JPY at 1.01, EUR/JPY at 1.84 — the cross costs roughly as much as its two legs added together, which is what it should cost if the only way to make a price in it is to lay it off through the dollar. The same ordering runs through every other measure: EUR/JPY has the thinnest touch (3.5 mm against 4.1 and 4.4), the shallowest ten-level book (37 mm against ~50), the largest price impact (0.53 bps against 0.22), and the fewest trades (1,542 against 14,535).

2. The cross is quoted far more than it is traded. EUR/JPY carries 116 book messages per print, against 25 for EUR/USD and 30 for USD/JPY, despite being much the quietest pair. A market maker in the cross has to re-quote whenever either leg moves, so its message traffic is driven by the majors' volatility rather than by its own trading — an order-flow cost with no corresponding revenue, and part of why the cross is quoted wider.

3. Bounce and staleness pull the variance in opposite directions. At a fixed frequency, transaction RV exceeds midquote RV (EUR/USD at 1s: 2927 vs 2320 bps²) and transaction returns are negatively autocorrelated at lag 1 while midquote returns are not — textbook bid–ask bounce. But across frequencies the midquote signature rises rather than falls, because at one second 43–64% of midquote returns are exactly zero: with a one-pip spread and a tenth-pip tick, the EBS mid usually has not moved. The high-frequency RV is therefore biased down by discreteness, not up by noise, which is the opposite of the equity case and worth keeping in mind before quoting any one-second variance as an estimate of true volatility.

4. EUR/JPY's one-minute returns are strongly mean-reverting, and it is not simply non-trading. Its one-minute autocorrelation is −0.17 for the midquote and −0.15 for transactions, against essentially zero for both majors (t = −3.4 on 390 observations). Forward-filling is the obvious suspect, since the cross prints in only 79% of minutes against 97–100% for the majors — but that cannot explain the midquote figure, because EUR/JPY updates its quote 1.5 times a second and only 2.3% of its one-minute mid returns are zero. What fits instead is a transitory component in the cross's quoted mid: with a spread twice as wide and a book a quarter thinner, where the cross's mid sits inside its spread is itself noisy, and that noise reverses. The realized variance corroborates it — EUR/JPY's midquote RV falls from 2317 bps² at one minute to 1655 at five, as the transitory part averages out, while both majors rise over the same range. The practical reading is that the cross's mid is a materially noisier estimate of its efficient price than either major's, which is the same fact as its wider spread seen from the return side.

5. Triangular arbitrage exists, and is about as small as theory says it should be. Gross deviations appear in 0.39% of seconds across 63 episodes, with a median duration of one second (max seven), a mean edge of 0.29 bps and a median round-trip size of 0.77 mm EUR — about $3,100 for the whole session, before any cost, assuming all three legs fill in full at the quoted price. Charging a few EUR/JPY ticks per round trip roughly halves it. The edge is real rather than a sampling artefact: the quotes behind an opportunity are fresher than average (median stalest leg 1.4 s against 2.1 s), which is the opposite of the staleness signature. For scale: across all live seconds the median deviation is −1.58 bps, i.e. the triangle normally sits inside itself by about the width of the cross's own 1.84 bps spread, and even when it does open the mean edge is 0.29 bps — a sixth of that spread — with the largest of the day, 1.78 bps, still short of one full spread. The no-arbitrage relation therefore holds to within the cost of crossing the cross, and the residual is a latency race rather than a return available to a price-taker.

6. Both the deviations and the volatility cluster in the same window, and the window is the FOMC. The opportunities are concentrated in the first half hour (22 of the 91 open seconds) and after 13:00 (53 of 91), which is also where the day's largest moves sit — EUR/USD rallies 1.1% over the session, most of it between 12:25 and 14:30. The file carries no timezone, but the clock identifies itself: on 2012-01-25 the Committee released its first-ever rate projections at 14:00 ET, and EUR/USD drops 20 bps in the 14:00–14:01 minute exactly; the statement itself was scheduled for 12:30 ET, and the tape goes from zero prints in the 12:26 minute to 231 in 12:28 as the mid jumps 17 bps — so the timestamps are Eastern, and the day's volatility is the Fed's. The spread plot shows the same thing from the liquidity side: EUR/JPY's five-minute spread spikes to 2.6 bps in the 12:25 interval, its widest of the day, and impact λ in all three pairs peaks in the 12:30 and 14:00 intervals. The mechanism is the standard one: the triangle breaks when prices move fast enough that the three books adjust at different speeds, so arbitrage frequency is a symptom of information arriving, not of a market that is generally mispriced.

7. The intraday pattern is announcement-shaped rather than U-shaped. On the two majors the spread is narrowest late in the morning (0.68 bps for EUR/USD at 10:55, 0.77 for USD/JPY at 11:45) and widens through the afternoon, ending 30–40% wider than its morning low; the cross is different again, tightest in the first ten minutes and widest — 2.6 bps, twice its mean — in the 12:25 interval that contains the pre-statement jump. Depth shows no open-of-day trough at all: the thinnest five-minute touch on each pair falls mid-session (11:20, 13:55, 15:40), and EUR/JPY's touch is deepest at the open. Impact λ peaks on all three pairs in the 12:25 and 14:00 intervals, and the half-hourly variance of one-minute returns is five to ten times its mid-morning level in the 12:30–13:30 and 14:00–14:30 windows. FX has no opening auction and no overnight close on a 24-hour market, so the equity U-shape has no reason to appear; what shapes this day is the scheduled release, and the liquidity measures respond to it the way the models say — spreads and impact up, as the adverse-selection component rises when information arrives. The lag-1 autocorrelation of one-minute transaction returns is negative in most half hours, the bounce signature, but flips to +0.57 for EUR/USD in the 12:00–12:30 window, where the price trends into the release: at one-minute sampling a fast one-directional move reads as momentum, and the sign of the autocorrelation says which of the two effects, bounce or drift, is winning in that half hour.
